query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a moderate amount of zirconium (Zr) at a nominal x = 0.05 level into the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance the mechanical performance—specifically, increasing yield strength, compressive strength, hardness, and creep resistance—via lattice distortion and the precipitation of fine, coherent or semi-coherent Ni7Zr2-related particles, while also contributing to improved corrosion resistance compared to the Zr-free baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a ~70% FCC-dominant FCC + ordered B2 dual-phase lamellar microstructure produced from high-purity elements.
generation.intervention: Alloying with zirconium at x = 0.05 (with additional experiments at x = 0.01 and x = 0.1 for comparison), maintaining the as-cast processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Button ingots produced under Ar via cold-crucible/vacuum melting and remelted at least five times; mechanical tests performed at room temperature (compression at strain rate 1×10^-3 s^-1 on 3 mm × 6 mm cylinders, microhardness with 0.981 N load for 15 s), nanoindentation creep with a 10 mN peak load and a 100 s hold time; corrosion tests conducted after 30 min immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl with polarization scan from -0.8 to 1.5 V at 1 mV/s and EIS from 10^-2 to 10^4 Hz.
generation.structural_mediator: Moderate Zr addition promotes lattice distortion in the FCC/B2 matrix and leads to the formation of fine Ni- and Zr-rich Ni7Zr2 precipitates that appear as a discontinuous network—effectively bridging the FCC and B2 regions—thereby mediating the improved mechanical and corrosion properties.
generation.mechanism: The added Zr causes solid-solution strengthening through lattice distortion and, when present at x ≥ 0.05, forms fine, coherent or semi-coherent Ni7Zr2-related precipitates that impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding. Additionally, these precipitates and the resulting microstructural refinement can help form a more stable passive film (potentially containing ZrO2) which enhances corrosion resistance. An excess of Zr (x = 0.1) is expected to coarsen the precipitates, which would negatively affect mechanical behavior despite possibly improving corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline x = 0 alloy, the x = 0.05 alloy should exhibit increased hardness, higher yield and compressive strengths, and reduced room-temperature creep deformation due to effective dispersion and precipitation strengthening. While x = 0.1 may further improve corrosion resistance due to a more continuous Zr-rich phase forming a protective passive film, its mechanical properties are expected to be lower than those observed at x = 0.05.
generation.baseline: The x = 0 as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy shows an FCC + B2 lamellar structure with yield strength approximately 705 MPa, compressive strength of about 1183 MPa, and specific corrosion parameters (Icorr ≈ 0.09993 μA/cm², pitting potential ≈ 320.27 mV, corrosion rate ≈ 0.0011621 mm/year, charge-transfer resistance ≈ 2600 Ω·cm²).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is valid for as-cast Zr_xAlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys with x values of 0, 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1 produced under specified processing conditions, assessed at room temperature for mechanical testing and in 3.5 wt% NaCl for corrosion testing. The effects are expected in the context of the reported dual-phase (FCC+B2) microstructure and under the stated experimental conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative trends are supported by prior observations, the exact quantitative improvements in mechanical properties and the trade-off with corrosion resistance require further precision. Variability in processing and long-term stability under operational conditions (e.g., temperature fluctuations and sustained loads) remain as uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as-cast Zr_xAlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys for x = 0, 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1 under identical melting and casting conditions. Characterize the microstructure using XRD, SEM/EDS, and TEM/SAED to identify phase changes and precipitate formation. Conduct mechanical tests (microhardness, room-temperature compression, and nanoindentation creep) under the stated conditions to measure strength and creep resistance. Evaluate corrosion performance using potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
measurements: Phase identification and precipitate morphology via XRD, SEM/EDS, and TEM/SAED
Nanoindentation creep displacement and the estimation of stress exponent
Corrosion parameters including Icorr, Ecorr, pitting potential (Epit), corrosion rate, and charge-transfer resistance (Rct)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with x = 0.05 does not display a statistically significant improvement in mechanical properties (e.g., increased hardness, yield strength, compressive strength, and reduced creep deformation) relative to the x = 0 baseline, or if the predicted microstructural changes (fine Ni7Zr2 precipitation) are absent, then the hypothesis will be rejected. In addition, if the corrosion tests do not reflect the expected trend (i.e., x = 0.1 showing superior corrosion resistance due to a more continuous Zr-rich passive film) contrasting with mechanical performance, the hypothesis is falsified.
